title: Experiments with interacting ultracold polar molecules
authors: Philip D. Gregory, Jonathan M. Mortlock, Daniel K. Ruttley, Simon L. Cornish
abstract: Ultracold polar molecules have emerged as an exciting platform for experiments in quantum science, with many proposed applications seeking to leverage the existence of long-range dipolar interactions and the rich internal structure of long-lived states. However, the complexity of molecules also presents many experimental challenges. In this chapter, we review the experimental advances over the past two decades that have brought ultracold molecules under full quantum control. We focus on three key topics: control of ultracold molecular collisions, engineering dipolar interactions and nascent quantum simulations in optical lattices.
summary: This review surveys the experimental progress in harnessing ultracold polar molecules as a platform for quantum science. It details advanced techniques to achieve full quantum control, focusing specifically on managing long-range dipole-dipole interactions and minimizing loss during molecular collisions. The work highlights how these controlled systems can be used for complex quantum simulations.
main_problem: Reviewing experimental advances required to achieve full quantum control over ultracold polar molecules for applications like quantum simulation.
main_result: The review details successful techniques for controlling molecular collisions, engineering long-range dipolar interactions, and achieving precise internal state manipulation in these systems.
method: The paper reviews various experimental methods, including magnetoassociation, STIRAP transfer, and using optical lattices/tweezers to control interactions.
model_or_system: The system is ultracold polar diatomic molecules (e.g., bialkali species) possessing rich internal structure and long-range dipole-dipole interactions ($H_{dd}$). Control relies on manipulating rotational and hyperfine states via microwave or optical fields.
key_observables: Relative transition strengths, differential light shifts, collision loss rates, and the ability to prepare molecules in specific quantum superpositions.
important_parameters: Dipolar interaction strength ($V_{dd}$), magnetic field strength, laser detuning/wavelength (for magic angles/wavelengths), and temperature regime (ultracold).
main_assumptions: The review assumes the applicability of models like the rigid-rotor approximation and relies on external fields to induce or control dipole moments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Zeeman structures for bialkali molecules showing relative transition strengths versus magnetic field, and potentially show energy level diagrams related to molecular structure.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a review, focusing sequentially on three key areas: 1) Control of ultracold molecular collisions, 2) Engineering dipolar interactions using external fields/lattices, and 3) General internal state control mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work sits at the intersection of AMO physics and quantum simulation. The detailed discussion on controlling dipole-dipole interactions via magic wavelengths/angles is crucial for realizing coherent many-body dynamics in molecular systems.

The black solid lines indicate the energy of the free atom-molecule pair, while the red and blue lines show the energies from two different sets of possible NaK2 bound states. Fig. 5 Collisional shielding using circularly polarised microwaves, demonstrated between a pair of CaF molecules in the same optical tweezer trap. (a) The presence of the microwaves forms two dressed states that diverge as a function of the intermolecular separation due to the dipole-dipole interaction. Coupling to the upper state results in a repulsive interaction that prevents the molecules from reaching short range and thus suppressing collisional loss, while coupling to the lower state enhances the loss. (b) The lifetime of the molecule-pair in the ground state to those prepared in either of the dressed states. Source: (a, b) are adapted from Ref. [143].
